cards.back: Ductus venosus past the liver, foramen ovale between atria, ductus arteriosus from pulmonary artery to aorta. The first breath drops pulmonary resistance, raising left atrial pressure and oxygen, closing them.

cards.front: What do central chemoreceptors actually sense?
cards.back: Not CO2 directly. CO2 crosses into CSF, forms carbonic acid, and lowers CSF pH, which is what the ventral medullary receptors read. They dominate normal breathing drive.

cards.front: When do peripheral chemoreceptors take over, and where are they?
cards.back: Carotid and aortic bodies. They respond weakly until PaO2 falls below about 60 mmHg, then drive hard. They also sense acidosis, the pathway behind Kussmaul breathing.

cards.front: What oxygen target is used in COPD, and what is the real mechanism of oxygen-induced hypercapnia?
cards.back: Titrate to SpO2 88 to 92%. The main mechanism is loss of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction worsening V/Q matching, plus the Haldane effect, not simply suppressed drive. Never withhold oxygen from a hypoxic patient.

cards.front: Name the breathing pattern for each: DKA, low cardiac output, medullary damage.
cards.back: Kussmaul (deep, fast, regular) in DKA. Cheyne-Stokes (crescendo, decrescendo, apnea) in low output or cerebral injury. Biot or ataxic (chaotic) in medullary damage.

cards.front: Distinguish type 1 from type 2 respiratory failure.
cards.back: Type 1 is hypoxemic: PaO2 under 60 with a normal or low PaCO2, an oxygenation failure. Type 2 is hypercapnic: PaCO2 over 45, a ventilation failure needing BiPAP or intubation, not more oxygen.

cards.front: What does the A-a gradient tell you, and what is normal?
cards.back: A normal gradient with hypoxemia means hypoventilation or low inspired oxygen; a widened one means the lung itself is failing. Normal is roughly age/4 + 4, about 9 at 20 and 19 at 60.

cards.front: Give the four-step ABG read with the normal values.
cards.back: pH 7.35 to 7.45, PaCO2 35 to 45, HCO3 22 to 26. Step 1 pH direction, step 2 does CO2 explain it, step 3 does HCO3 explain it, step 4 is the other value compensating.

cards.front: How do you calculate the anion gap and what does a raised one mean?
cards.back: Na minus (Cl + HCO3), normal 8 to 12. A raised gap means unmeasured acid was added: MUDPILES. A normal gap means bicarbonate was lost, as in severe diarrhea or renal tubular acidosis.

quiz.q: Which event produces the first heart sound, S1?
choices: Closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves
Opening of the aortic and pulmonic valves
Closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves
Atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle
quiz.why: All normal heart sounds are valves closing. S1 is the AV valves at the start of systole. Choice 3 is S2 and choice 4 is S4. Valve opening is silent unless the valve is diseased.

quiz.q: A 24-year-old is stabbed in the left chest. BP 76/60, HR 132, neck veins distended, heart tones distant, breath sounds equal bilaterally. What is the mechanism of the hypotension?
choices: Loss of circulating volume from external hemorrhage
Loss of systemic vascular resistance from spinal injury
Pericardial blood preventing ventricular filling
Air under pressure collapsing the left lung
quiz.why: Beck's triad with equal breath sounds is tamponade: as little as 150 to 200 mL in the non-compliant sac destroys preload. Tension pneumothorax would give absent breath sounds on one side. Hemorrhagic shock gives flat neck veins, and neurogenic shock gives bradycardia with warm skin.

quiz.q: A murmur is heard between S1 and S2. Which lesion is most consistent?
choices: Mitral stenosis
Aortic stenosis
Aortic regurgitation
Pulmonic regurgitation
quiz.why: Between S1 and S2 is systole, when the semilunar valves should be open and the AV valves shut. So a systolic murmur means either forward flow through a narrowed semilunar valve (aortic stenosis) or backward leak through an AV valve. The other three choices are diastolic murmurs.

quiz.q: In roughly 85 to 90 percent of people, which artery supplies the AV node?
choices: Left anterior descending
Left circumflex
Left main
Right coronary artery
quiz.why: The RCA supplies the AV node in about 85 to 90% and the SA node in about 60% of people, along with the inferior wall and right ventricle. The LAD feeds the anterior wall and septum; the circumflex feeds the lateral wall.

quiz.q: A 58-year-old has ST elevation in II, III and aVF, HR 48, BP 88/56, clear lungs and distended neck veins. Which action is most appropriate?
choices: Give sublingual nitroglycerin for the chest pain
Obtain a right-sided ECG and give a fluid bolus for hypotension
Give IV furosemide for the elevated neck veins
Start a nitroglycerin drip to reduce afterload
quiz.why: Inferior ST elevation plus bradycardia, hypotension, clear lungs and JVD is right ventricular infarction. The RV depends on preload, so nitrates or diuretics can cause catastrophic hypotension. V4R confirms it, and volume is the supportive treatment.

quiz.q: ST elevation is present in V3 and V4. Which wall and artery does this represent?
choices: Lateral wall, circumflex
Inferior wall, right coronary artery
Anterior wall, left anterior descending
Posterior wall, circumflex
quiz.why: V3 and V4 are the anterior leads, supplied by the LAD; V1 and V2 are septal, also LAD. Lateral is I, aVL, V5 and V6, and inferior is II, III and aVF. Posterior injury shows as tall R waves with ST depression in V1 to V3.

quiz.q: Cardiac output is calculated as which of the following?
choices: Stroke volume multiplied by heart rate
Mean arterial pressure divided by heart rate
End-diastolic volume minus end-systolic volume
Systolic pressure minus diastolic pressure
quiz.why: CO = SV x HR, about 70 mL x 70 beats, or roughly 5 L/min at rest. Choice 3 defines stroke volume itself, and choice 4 defines pulse pressure. MAP is CO multiplied by SVR, not divided by rate.

quiz.q: A patient's blood pressure is 96/60. What is the approximate mean arterial pressure?
choices: 60 mmHg
68 mmHg
78 mmHg
72 mmHg
quiz.why: MAP = DBP + 1/3(SBP - DBP) = 60 + 1/3(36) = 60 + 12 = 72 mmHg. Choosing the diastolic alone or the simple average of the two numbers are the common errors; the diastolic is weighted more because diastole occupies about two-thirds of the cycle.

quiz.q: A patient in decompensated heart failure receives 2 L of saline and becomes more dyspneic with new crackles. Which physiologic principle explains this?
choices: Increased afterload reduced ejection fraction
Increased contractility raised myocardial oxygen demand
The ventricle is beyond the peak of the Frank-Starling curve, so added preload backs up into the lungs
Increased systemic vascular resistance reduced venous return
quiz.why: Frank-Starling says more stretch yields a stronger squeeze only up to a point. An already overstretched failing ventricle sits past the peak, so extra volume raises filling pressure without raising stroke volume, and that pressure transmits back into the pulmonary capillaries.

quiz.q: Which intervention primarily reduces afterload?
choices: A 500 mL crystalloid bolus
An arterial vasodilator lowering systemic vascular resistance
Atropine raising the heart rate
Placing the patient in Trendelenburg position
quiz.why: Afterload is the pressure the ventricle must overcome to eject, dominated by SVR. Arterial vasodilation lowers it. Fluid and positioning change preload, and atropine changes rate, neither of which is afterload.

quiz.q: What is the intrinsic firing rate of the AV junction when the SA node fails?
choices: 40 to 60 beats per minute
20 to 40 beats per minute
60 to 100 beats per minute
100 to 120 beats per minute
quiz.why: The hierarchy is SA node 60 to 100, AV junction 40 to 60, and ventricular or Purkinje escape 20 to 40. A rate in the 30s with no P waves means a ventricular escape rhythm has taken over.

quiz.q: A dialysis patient who missed two sessions has tall, narrow, peaked T waves and a widening QRS. Which treatment stabilizes the myocardium fastest without changing the serum level?
choices: Regular insulin with dextrose
Nebulized albuterol
Sodium polystyrene sulfonate
IV calcium gluconate
quiz.why: Calcium raises the threshold potential and stabilizes the membrane within minutes but does not move potassium at all. Insulin with dextrose and albuterol shift potassium into cells, and binders or dialysis remove it, all of which are slower.

quiz.q: An 18-year-old ingested amitriptyline. The QRS is 168 ms and the patient is hypotensive. Which mechanism explains the ECG finding, and what treats it?
choices: Potassium efflux blockade; give magnesium
Calcium channel blockade; give calcium chloride
Fast sodium channel blockade; give sodium bicarbonate
Beta receptor blockade; give glucagon
quiz.why: Tricyclics block the fast sodium channel that drives phase 0, slowing ventricular depolarization and widening the QRS. Bicarbonate provides a sodium load and raises pH, both of which push sodium through the channel. Glucagon is for beta blocker overdose and calcium for calcium channel blocker overdose.

quiz.q: What is the physiologic purpose of the delay at the AV node?
choices: It limits the maximum sinus rate
It gives the atria time to finish filling the ventricles before they contract
It generates the calcium plateau of phase 2
It produces ventricular repolarization
quiz.why: The roughly 0.1 second delay is why atrial kick contributes its 20 to 30% of filling. It makes up most of the PR interval, normally 0.12 to 0.20 s. Repolarization and the plateau are ion events in the myocyte, not nodal functions.

quiz.q: A patient with nephrotic syndrome has an albumin of 1.6 g/dL and pitting edema of both legs. Which Starling force is deranged?
choices: Reduced plasma oncotic pressure
Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure
Increased capillary permeability
Obstructed lymphatic drainage
quiz.why: Albumin generates the roughly 25 mmHg oncotic pull that returns fluid at the venous end. Losing it in the urine drops that pull. Hydrostatic pressure rises in heart failure or venous obstruction, permeability rises in sepsis and burns, and lymphatic obstruction follows node dissection.

quiz.q: Which vessels are primarily responsible for systemic vascular resistance?
choices: Elastic arteries such as the aorta
Capillaries
Large veins
Arterioles
quiz.why: Arterioles are nearly all smooth muscle and resistance varies with the fourth power of radius, so they set SVR. The aorta buffers pulsatile flow, capillaries exchange, and veins hold 60 to 70% of the blood volume as capacitance.

quiz.q: A soldier faints after standing at attention for 40 minutes in the heat. Which mechanism best explains it?
choices: Loss of arterial elasticity raised pulse pressure
Capillary permeability increased from heat
Venous pooling reduced preload because the muscle pump was not being used
Aldosterone secretion dropped acutely
quiz.why: Veins hold most of the blood volume and depend on calf muscle contraction plus one-way valves to return it uphill. Standing motionless removes that pump, blood pools, preload falls, stroke volume falls, and cerebral perfusion drops. Heat adds vasodilation to the problem.

quiz.q: A patient has lost about 1200 mL of blood. HR 124, BP 116/94, skin cool and pale. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: The pressure is normal, so perfusion is adequate
The baroreflex is defending the pressure with tachycardia and vasoconstriction; this is compensated shock
The narrow pulse pressure indicates neurogenic shock
RAAS has already restored the lost volume
quiz.why: A pulse pressure of 22 with cool skin means arteriolar constriction is holding the diastolic up. This is the baroreflex, and it usually keeps pressure normal until roughly 30% of volume is lost. Neurogenic shock would show bradycardia with warm dry skin, and RAAS acts over hours, not minutes.

quiz.q: At which step of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system does lisinopril act?
choices: Conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II
Binding of angiotensin II to its receptor
Aldosterone action at the distal tubule
Renin release from juxtaglomerular cells
quiz.why: ACE inhibitors block angiotensin converting enzyme, mostly in pulmonary endothelium. Because ACE also degrades bradykinin, blocking it causes the dry cough and angioedema. Receptor blockade is an ARB and aldosterone blockade is spironolactone.

quiz.q: A 74-year-old is dyspneic. BNP returns at 1450 pg/mL. What does this most support?
choices: Pulmonary embolism as the cause
A COPD exacerbation
Pneumonia with sepsis
Ventricular wall stretch from volume overload, supporting acute heart failure
quiz.why: BNP is released by stretched ventricular myocardium and opposes RAAS. A value under about 100 pg/mL argues strongly against acute heart failure; values over 400 to 500 support it. Age and renal failure raise it independently, so it supports rather than proves the diagnosis.

quiz.q: A patient has BP 78/34, HR 118, warm dry flushed skin, flat neck veins, lactate 4.8 mmol/L and a temperature of 39.1 C. Which hemodynamic profile fits?
choices: High SVR, low cardiac output, high preload
High SVR, low cardiac output, low preload
Low SVR, high cardiac output, low effective preload
Low SVR, low cardiac output, high preload
quiz.why: Fever plus warm skin, a wide pulse pressure and flat neck veins is distributive shock: vasodilation drops SVR while output rises early to compensate. High SVR with low preload would be hypovolemic and cool; high SVR with high preload would be cardiogenic and congested.

quiz.q: Which bedside finding best distinguishes cardiogenic shock from hypovolemic shock?
choices: Tachycardia
Distended jugular veins with pulmonary crackles
Cool, clammy skin
Delayed capillary refill
quiz.why: Both states trigger the same sympathetic response, so tachycardia, cool skin and slow refill appear in both. The difference is preload: a failing pump backs blood up, filling the neck veins and wetting the lungs, while hemorrhage empties them.

quiz.q: What does an elevated serum lactate indicate?
choices: Anaerobic metabolism from inadequate tissue oxygen delivery
Excess oxygen delivery to tissues
Renal failure to excrete bicarbonate
Hyperventilation blowing off carbon dioxide
quiz.why: Cells without oxygen convert pyruvate to lactate instead of entering the mitochondria, so lactate is a direct readout of hypoperfusion. Normal is under 2 mmol/L and over 4 marks severe hypoperfusion. Clearance of 10 to 20% after resuscitation is the reassuring trend.

quiz.q: A septic patient remains at MAP 58 mmHg after 30 mL/kg of crystalloid. Which vasopressor is first-line?
choices: Dopamine
Phenylephrine
Dobutamine
Norepinephrine
quiz.why: Septic shock is chiefly a loss of SVR, so an alpha-1 dominant agent is the physiologic match. Norepinephrine produces fewer tachyarrhythmias than dopamine at equal pressure support. Dobutamine is an inotrope that can drop pressure further, and phenylephrine is a later alternative.

quiz.q: Approximately how large is anatomic dead space in an average adult?
choices: 50 mL
500 mL
150 mL
quiz.why: Dead space is roughly 2 mL/kg, about 150 mL, the volume of the conducting airways from nose to terminal bronchioles where no exchange occurs. 500 mL is a typical tidal volume and 1200 mL is residual volume.

quiz.q: A patient breathes at a rate of 36 with tidal volumes of about 200 mL. Which statement is correct?
choices: Minute ventilation is low, so hypercapnia is expected
Minute ventilation is about 7.2 L/min but alveolar ventilation is only about 1.8 L/min
Alveolar ventilation is normal because the rate compensates
Dead space is irrelevant at high respiratory rates
quiz.why: Minute ventilation is 200 x 36 = 7200 mL, which looks normal. Alveolar ventilation is (200 - 150) x 36 = 1800 mL, severely inadequate, because dead space is subtracted from every single breath. Rapid shallow breathing is the least efficient pattern there is.

quiz.q: A 38-week pregnant patient desaturates within 30 seconds of apnea despite 3 minutes of preoxygenation. Why?
choices: Functional residual capacity is reduced, shrinking the stored oxygen reservoir
Tidal volume is reduced, so less oxygen was inhaled
Anatomic dead space is doubled in pregnancy
Hemoglobin binds oxygen more tightly in pregnancy
quiz.why: The gravid uterus pushes the diaphragm up and eliminates much of the expiratory reserve volume, so FRC falls by roughly 20%. FRC is the oxygen the lungs hold between breaths, so a smaller FRC shortens safe apnea time. Tidal volume and minute ventilation actually increase in pregnancy.

quiz.q: An SpO2 of 90 percent corresponds to approximately what PaO2?
choices: 100 mmHg
80 mmHg
40 mmHg
60 mmHg
quiz.why: The landmark points are PaO2 100 equals about 98%, PaO2 60 equals about 90%, and PaO2 40 equals about 75%. An SpO2 of 90% sits at the top of the steep portion of the curve, which is why further small drops collapse the saturation quickly.

quiz.q: Two hypoxemic patients: one has a clear chest x-ray, sudden dyspnea and EtCO2 of 24; the other has a dense lobar consolidation and SpO2 that will not rise on 100 percent oxygen. What distinguishes their V/Q abnormalities?
choices: Both are shunt; only the severity differs
Both are dead space; only the severity differs
The first is dead space from a clot; the second is shunt, which does not correct with oxygen
The first is shunt; the second is dead space
quiz.why: Dead space is ventilation without perfusion, so a pulmonary embolism gives a low EtCO2 with a clear film and partial response to oxygen. Shunt is perfusion without ventilation, so consolidated lung passes blood that oxygen never reaches, and the hypoxemia is refractory.

quiz.q: A septic patient has a temperature of 39.5 C, pH 7.24 and elevated 2,3-DPG. What happens to the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve?
choices: It shifts left, so hemoglobin holds oxygen more tightly
It shifts right, so hemoglobin releases oxygen more readily at the tissue
It flattens, eliminating cooperative binding
It is unchanged, because pH affects only CO2 transport
quiz.why: CADET face right: CO2, acid, 2,3-DPG, exercise and temperature all shift the curve right, which unloads oxygen where metabolism is highest. Left shifts come from hypothermia, alkalosis, low DPG, carbon monoxide and fetal hemoglobin.

quiz.q: Interpret this arterial blood gas: pH 7.19, PaCO2 58 mmHg, HCO3 23 mEq/L.
choices: Uncompensated respiratory acidosis
Partially compensated metabolic acidosis
Fully compensated respiratory acidosis
Uncompensated metabolic alkalosis
quiz.why: The pH is acidemic, the PaCO2 is elevated and explains it, and the bicarbonate is still normal, meaning the kidneys have not had time to compensate. Full compensation would show a normal pH with both values abnormal, and a metabolic cause would show a low bicarbonate.

quiz.q: An opioid overdose patient on 15 L by non-rebreather has SpO2 98 percent, RR 6 and EtCO2 rising from 42 to 78. What is the correct interpretation and action?
choices: Adequate oxygenation and ventilation; continue to observe
Type 1 hypoxemic failure; increase the oxygen flow rate
The EtCO2 monitor is reading the oxygen flow incorrectly
Type 2 hypercapnic failure; the saturation is propped up by oxygen, so assist ventilation
quiz.why: Oxygenation and ventilation are separate. High-flow oxygen keeps saturation near normal long after the patient has stopped clearing CO2, so the SpO2 is falsely reassuring. A climbing EtCO2 with a rate of 6 is ventilatory failure, treated with assisted ventilation and naloxone, not more oxygen.

scenarios.title: Reasoning it out: which shock is this?
scenarios.intro:
No treatment decisions here. You are going to take one hypotensive patient and walk the equation `MAP = CO x SVR` until the numbers tell you which term failed. Work the physiology at each step before you pick.

The case: a 61-year-old woman brought in from home for three days of fever and cough, now confused. You have vitals, a physical exam, and one lab.

steps.prompt: Here is what you have on arrival. Before you name a shock type, decide which side of `MAP = CO x SVR` you can actually assess with these numbers.

choices.text: Compute the MAP and the pulse pressure first, because both are derived from what you already have
choices.feedback: Right. MAP is 36 + 1/3(44), about 51 mmHg, well under the 65 floor. Pulse pressure is 44 on a mean of 51, which is wide relative to the mean. A wide pulse pressure with a low mean points at low resistance, not low volume.

choices.text: Call it hypovolemic shock, because the heart rate is 124 and the pressure is low
choices.feedback: Too fast. Tachycardia and hypotension appear in every shock state, because the baroreflex answers all of them the same way. The vital signs alone cannot separate them, which is exactly why you compute derived numbers and then examine the skin.

choices.text: Wait for a lactate before doing anything else
choices.feedback: The lactate is coming and it will confirm hypoperfusion, but it will not tell you which term failed. Lactate answers how bad, not which kind. Do the arithmetic you already have.

steps.prompt:
You examine her. Skin is warm and flushed at the chest and dry. Capillary refill is `2 seconds`. Neck veins are flat with the head of bed at `30 degrees`. Lungs have coarse crackles at the right base only.

What does warm, flushed skin with flat neck veins tell you about SVR and preload?

choices.text: SVR is low and preload is low; the vessels have dilated and the circuit is underfilled
choices.feedback: Correct, and notice how you got there. Warm skin means the arterioles did not constrict, so SVR is the failed term. Flat neck veins mean the right heart is not backed up, so this is not a pump or an obstruction problem.

choices.text: SVR is high and preload is high; this is a failing pump
choices.feedback: That profile exists, but it looks completely different: cool mottled skin from compensatory vasoconstriction, plus distended neck veins and diffuse crackles from blood backing up. Warm and flat is the opposite picture.

choices.text: SVR is high and preload is low; she is simply dehydrated from three days of illness
choices.feedback: Dehydration is certainly contributing, and in high SVR states the skin is cool and clamped with a narrow pulse pressure. Hers is warm with a wide pulse pressure, so resistance has failed on top of any volume deficit.

choices.text: The exam cannot assess SVR without an arterial line
choices.feedback: A number would be nice, but skin temperature, capillary refill and pulse pressure are a reliable clinical surrogate for vascular tone, and they are available at the bedside in seconds. Learn to read them.

steps.prompt:
Lactate returns at `5.2 mmol/L`. A chest film shows a right lower lobe infiltrate.

Put the whole fingerprint together. Which shock state, and what is the CO doing early in it?

choices.text: Distributive shock from sepsis; cardiac output is typically high early as the heart compensates for the collapsed SVR
choices.feedback: Exactly. The classic early septic profile is high output, low resistance, warm periphery. That is why it was once called warm shock. Late in the course, myocardial depression and capillary leak drive output down and the patient turns cool.

choices.text: Obstructive shock; the infiltrate is compressing the right heart
choices.feedback: An infiltrate does not obstruct the circuit. Obstructive shock means tension pneumothorax, tamponade or massive pulmonary embolism, and all three raise SVR and give cool skin with distended neck veins.

choices.text: Cardiogenic shock; the lactate of 5.2 proves the pump has failed
choices.feedback: Lactate rises in every shock state because it measures anaerobic metabolism, not pump function. Over 4 mmol/L tells you the hypoperfusion is severe; it does not name the cause.

steps.prompt:
Now reason about treatment strictly from the physiology, not from a protocol you have memorized.

The failed term is SVR, and the circuit is underfilled because the capillaries are leaking. Which sequence follows from that?

choices.text: Fill the circuit first with about `30 mL/kg` of balanced crystalloid, then add an alpha-1 agonist if MAP stays under `65`
choices.feedback: Correct, and the order matters mechanically. Squeezing an empty circuit raises pressure by shrinking the container while flow stays low, which can look better on the monitor and perfuse less. Volume first, tone second.

choices.text: Start norepinephrine immediately and give no fluid, since the problem is resistance
choices.feedback: Tempting logic, but capillary leak means the intravascular space is genuinely empty even though the tissues are wet. A vasopressor into an empty tank raises numbers without raising delivery. Fluid comes first unless the patient is already overloaded.

choices.text: Give furosemide because there are crackles on the chest exam
choices.feedback: Those crackles are pneumonia, not volume overload. Flat neck veins and a wide pulse pressure argue against congestion. Diuresing a septic, underfilled patient makes the perfusion worse.

choices.text: Give a fluid bolus and start dobutamine to raise cardiac output
choices.feedback: Dobutamine is an inotrope with beta-2 vasodilating activity, so it can drop SVR further. Her contractility is not the failed term; her resistance is. Save inotropes for when output stays low after tone and volume are addressed.

steps.prompt:
Last step, and it is the generalization. Someone hands you a different hypotensive patient: `BP 84/40`, `HR 46`, skin warm, dry and pink, neck veins flat, after a fall from a roof.

Which term failed here, and what makes this one recognizable?

choices.text: SVR failed, and the giveaway is hypotension with bradycardia and warm dry skin, meaning sympathetic outflow itself is cut
choices.feedback: That is neurogenic shock from a cord injury above roughly T6. It is the only shock state that cannot mount a compensatory tachycardia, because the sympathetic chain that would produce it has been interrupted. Hemorrhage still has to be excluded in a trauma patient.

choices.text: Preload failed from hemorrhage; the bradycardia is a terminal finding
choices.feedback: Hemorrhage must be ruled out in any fall, and both can coexist. But hemorrhagic shock produces tachycardia with cool, pale, clammy skin until very late. Warm, dry, pink skin with bradycardia points at lost sympathetic tone.

choices.text: Contractility failed; this is cardiogenic shock from blunt cardiac injury
choices.feedback: Blunt cardiac injury is real after a fall, but cardiogenic shock backs blood up: distended neck veins, crackles, cool mottled skin. Flat neck veins with warm skin is the opposite fingerprint.

scenarios.debrief:
The pattern to keep: every shock is one term of `MAP = CO x SVR` failing, and the bedside exam reads the terms directly.

Skin temperature reports SVR. Warm means resistance failed (distributive, neurogenic). Cool means the body is compensating by constricting, so the problem is volume or pump.

Neck veins report preload on the right side. Flat means the circuit is underfilled (hypovolemic, distributive). Distended means something is blocking or backing up (cardiogenic, obstructive).

Pulse pressure reports stroke volume against tone. Narrow means low volume with tight vessels. Wide on a low mean means dilated vessels.

Lactate reports how badly tissue is starving, never which term failed. And a MAP under `65 mmHg` is the line where organs stop autoregulating, which is why you compute it instead of reading the systolic.

scenarios.title: Two gases, four steps
scenarios.intro:
You will read two arterial blood gases using the same four steps every time: pH, then PaCO2, then HCO3, then compensation. No shortcuts and no pattern matching.

Normals to hold in mind: `pH 7.35` to `7.45`, `PaCO2 35` to `45 mmHg`, `HCO3 22` to `26 mEq/L`. Remember that CO2 behaves as an acid and bicarbonate as a base.

steps.prompt:
Gas one, from a 22-year-old with type 1 diabetes who has been vomiting for two days and is breathing deeply at a rate of `32`.

`pH 7.18`, `PaCO2 22 mmHg`, `HCO3 8 mEq/L`, `Na 138`, `Cl 99`.

Step one: what does the pH tell you?

choices.text: Acidemia, and it is severe, so one of the other two values has to be the cause
choices.feedback: Correct. 7.18 is well below 7.35. Naming the direction first is what keeps you from guessing later, because whichever value moved the same way as the pH is the primary disorder.

choices.text: Alkalemia, because the PaCO2 is low
choices.feedback: Step one is the pH itself, not an inference from another value. The pH is 7.18, which is acidemic. The low PaCO2 will turn out to be compensation, and reading it first is exactly how people get these backwards.

choices.text: Normal pH with two abnormal values, so it is fully compensated
choices.feedback: Full compensation does look like that, but only when the pH is actually back inside 7.35 to 7.45. At 7.18 nothing has been compensated successfully.

steps.prompt:
Steps two and three: check each value against the acidemia. `PaCO2 22` is low. `HCO3 8` is low.

Which one explains an acidemia?

choices.text: The low bicarbonate; a low base explains a low pH, while a low CO2 would raise the pH
choices.feedback: Exactly the logic. CO2 is an acid, so losing it should push pH up. Bicarbonate is a base, so losing it pushes pH down. The value that moves the pH in the observed direction is the primary disorder: metabolic acidosis.

choices.text: The low PaCO2, because low CO2 means poor ventilation
choices.feedback: Low CO2 means more ventilation, not less, and it produces alkalosis rather than acidosis. She is breathing at 32 with deep Kussmaul respirations precisely to blow CO2 off.

choices.text: Both, equally
choices.feedback: They cannot both be primary here because they push pH in opposite directions. One is the disorder and one is the response. Ask which direction each value moves the pH, and the answer resolves itself.

steps.prompt:
Step four, plus the extra step that metabolic acidosis always earns.

The pH is still `7.18` despite a `PaCO2` of `22`. And you have `Na 138`, `Cl 99`, `HCO3 8`.

choices.text: Partially compensated metabolic acidosis, anion gap 31, so unmeasured acid has been added
choices.feedback: Right on both counts. Compensation is present but incomplete because the pH is still abnormal. Anion gap is 138 - (99 + 8) = 31, far above the normal 8 to 12, which means acid was added rather than bicarbonate lost. With this history, ketoacids.

choices.text: Fully compensated metabolic acidosis with a normal anion gap
choices.feedback: Neither part holds. Full compensation requires a pH back inside 7.35 to 7.45, and the gap is 31, not normal. A normal-gap acidosis would suggest bicarbonate losses from diarrhea or renal tubular acidosis instead.

choices.text: Uncompensated metabolic acidosis with a raised anion gap
choices.feedback: The gap of 31 is correct, but uncompensated would mean the PaCO2 had not moved. It is 22, well below 35, so the lungs are working hard at compensating. Partially compensated is the accurate label.

choices.text: Mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis, since both values are low
choices.feedback: This is the sophisticated trap. A low CO2 alongside a metabolic acidosis is expected compensation, not a second primary disorder. You would only call it mixed if the CO2 had fallen much further than compensation predicts, which is what the Winter formula checks.

steps.prompt:
Gas two, from a 68-year-old with severe COPD who is at his baseline, talking in full sentences, here for a wrist fracture.

`pH 7.36`, `PaCO2 62 mmHg`, `HCO3 34 mEq/L`.

Run the same four steps. What is this?

choices.text: Fully compensated respiratory acidosis, the expected chronic COPD picture
choices.feedback: Correct. pH is in range but sitting on the acid side of 7.40, which tells you which disorder is primary. The CO2 is high and matches that leaning, and the kidneys have retained enough bicarbonate over weeks to pull the pH back into range.

choices.text: Fully compensated metabolic alkalosis
choices.feedback: The arithmetic looks the same but the primary is chosen by which side of 7.40 the pH sits on. At 7.36 it leans acidemic, so the acid-side value, the CO2, is the primary problem. A primary metabolic alkalosis would have a pH above 7.40.

choices.text: Acute respiratory failure requiring immediate intubation
choices.feedback: A PaCO2 of 62 in isolation looks alarming, but the near-normal pH and the raised bicarbonate prove this took weeks to develop. He is talking in full sentences at his baseline. Treat the patient, not the number.

steps.prompt:
Same patient, three hours later, after he was given high-flow oxygen and some opioid for the fracture. He is now drowsy.

`pH 7.19`, `PaCO2 88 mmHg`, `HCO3 35 mEq/L`.

What changed, and what does it mean?

choices.text: Acute respiratory acidosis on top of chronic: the CO2 jumped while bicarbonate barely moved, so this is an acute ventilatory failure needing ventilatory support
choices.feedback: That is the reasoning. Renal compensation takes days, so a bicarbonate that is nearly unchanged while CO2 climbs 26 points proves the change is acute. Drowsiness with a pH of 7.19 is type 2 respiratory failure, and the treatment is ventilation, whether BiPAP or a tube.

choices.text: A new metabolic acidosis, since the pH fell
choices.feedback: The bicarbonate went up, not down, so no base was lost. When bicarbonate is high and pH is low, the acid has to be respiratory. Watch the direction of each value rather than only the pH.

choices.text: Worsening chronic retention, expected in COPD, so continue observation
choices.feedback: Chronic retention does not drop the pH to 7.19, because the kidneys keep pace over days. The gap between a big CO2 rise and an unchanged bicarbonate is exactly how you identify an acute change on a chronic background.

choices.text: Oxygen toxicity destroyed the hypoxic drive, so oxygen should be stopped entirely
choices.feedback: Half right and dangerously applied. Oxygen-induced hypercapnia is real, driven mostly by loss of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction worsening V/Q matching plus the Haldane effect. The answer is to titrate to an SpO2 of 88 to 92% and support ventilation, never to remove oxygen from a hypoxic patient.

scenarios.debrief:
The four steps never change: pH direction, then does the CO2 explain it, then does the bicarbonate explain it, then is the other value compensating.

Two habits make it automatic. First, decide which value moved the pH in the direction it actually went. CO2 up or bicarbonate down both mean acidosis; CO2 down or bicarbonate up both mean alkalosis. Second, when the pH is normal but both values are abnormal, the primary disorder is named by whichever side of `7.40` the pH is leaning toward.

Compensation has a timescale. The lungs respond to a metabolic problem within minutes. The kidneys take `24` to `72 hours` to respond to a respiratory problem. So a high CO2 with a high bicarbonate is chronic, and a high CO2 with a normal bicarbonate is acute, and the difference decides whether the patient needs watching or a ventilator.

Every metabolic acidosis gets an anion gap, `Na - (Cl + HCO3)`, normal `8` to `12`. Raised means acid was added, MUDPILES. Normal means bicarbonate was lost.
